Bhante, what is the role of Anattā (Not-Self) in dismantling linguistic delusion in 'Concept and Reality'?

Anattā is the surgical blade that severs the root of linguistic delusion. When you see that all five aggregates are changing processes devoid of an 'I', the entire grammatical fortress of 'me' and 'mine' crumbles. There is seeing, but no seer; there is thinking, but no thinker. It is like discovering that the scary shadow on the wall was cast by an empty coat hanger. Walk in the unburdened freedom of not-self.

Bhante, how does 'Concept and Reality' describe the transition from worldling to noble disciple?

The worldling is an uninstructed prisoner of language, taking conceptual boundaries as absolute dogmas. The noble disciple (*ariya-sāvaka*), having seen the rise and fall of the aggregates, recognizes concepts as mere tools. The noble disciple uses language without being used by it, dwelling in the signless peace of Nibbāna. It is like a master carpenter using a saw: he cuts the wood skillfully, but does not carry the saw to bed. Use concepts skillfully and abide in peace.
